opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think a lot of the SLAM work that matters most for what I do isn't coming out of the traditional SLAM community anymore, at least not in the classic sense. The core geometric SLAM problem, localizing a mobile robot or a car in a large environment, is in many ways quite mature. The self-driving and AR/VR industries have pushed it really far, and companies building headsets and glasses have invested enormously in robust, low-power visual-inertial tracking. That's where the most battle-tested engineering is happening.

But for robot manipulation, which is my focus, the needs are a bit different. I don't just need to know where the camera is. I need to understand the scene at the level of objects: what they are, how they can move, how they'd respond if I push or grasp them. So the work I find most useful sits at the intersection of 3D vision and learning: neural scene representations, things like NeRFs and Gaussian splatting, and the newer 3D foundation models that can reconstruct geometry and camera pose from just a few images in a single feed-forward pass. A lot of that is coming from computer vision groups and big industry labs, not robotics labs specifically.

One more area I'm really excited about is egocentric data. If you want to learn manipulation from human videos, say someone wearing smart glasses while cooking, you need to accurately track the head, the hands, and the objects in 3D over time. That's essentially a SLAM problem plus hand and object tracking, and the wearable device companies are building that infrastructure at scale. For us, that's very valuable, because it turns everyday human activity into training data for robots.

So if I had to summarize: classic SLAM is being refined in industry, in AR/VR and autonomous driving, but the version that's most useful for robot learning is emerging from the merger of SLAM with deep learning and 3D foundation models, and it's increasingly object-centric and semantic rather than purely geometric.

r001.rationale: The response says AR/VR companies have invested in robust tracking, but it does not claim sub-centimeter precision or that this capability exists only at AR/VR companies; it also mentions autonomous-driving industry work.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a good question, because honestly most of the SLAM I rely on isn't being developed in my lab at all. My work at Georgia Tech is about robot learning for manipulation, so we're focused on how a robot grasps, rearranges, and chains together long-horizon tasks in a kitchen or a lab. SLAM is the thing we depend on so we can even start asking those questions.

If I'm being candid, the most useful progress is coming from a few different places. There's the classic academic robotics community, groups like the ones at ETH Zurich, TUM, and MIT, who built the foundations with ORB-SLAM, Kimera, and the dense RGB-D systems. Then there's the industry side, places like Apple, Meta, and the AR headset teams, who have poured enormous resources into making visual-inertial tracking run robustly on a phone or a headset. A lot of that has quietly become the backbone of what hobbyists and research labs can bootstrap from.

And the newest piece, which I find most exciting for our side of things, is the merger of SLAM with learning-based 3D representations. Neural fields, Gaussian splatting, feed-forward models that reconstruct a scene from a few frames. Those are coming out of groups at Stanford, Berkeley, and a bunch of startups, and they matter to us because manipulation doesn't just need to know where the robot is. It needs a representation of the scene that a policy can actually reason over, including objects that move when you touch them. Classic SLAM assumes a static world, and a kitchen is anything but.

So the short answer is: the core localization is coming from the SLAM community and the AR industry, and the parts that are really changing how we do manipulation are coming from the learning-based 3D vision world. Our job is mostly to stitch those together and figure out what breaks when a robot starts interacting with the map instead of just observing it.

r001.rationale: The response credits AR companies with robust visual-inertial tracking, but does not state that sub-centimeter-precision SLAM exists only at AR/VR companies. It also describes academic groups as contributing SLAM foundations.

They’re tackling related problems: figuring out where a system is and building a useful map of its surroundings. For my work, the most useful direction is connecting that geometry to understanding—so a robot can recognize objects and reason about how to interact with them, rather than just know where they are.

For my work, what matters is moving beyond estimating where a robot is to understanding what’s around it—what the objects are and how the robot can interact with them. So I’m particularly interested in SLAM systems that build representations we can use for manipulation, especially when the environment changes.
